entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: ‘We Share This Loss’
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Nov. 16, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: The aftermath of the Logan Circle shooting, more East Potomac drama and the high-flying Spirit. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 6/10. There’s a chill in the air, especially early, but sunshine and afternoon temperatures in the 50s make for a pretty pleasant day. Read the full forecast.





THE LATEST

For hours last Thursday, he was the anonymous victim who was shot and killed during Dr. Matt Lambert’s spree of violence at a Logan Circle gym and condo building. Later, the police announced his name: James Stuart. To his friends, he was simply Jimmy.

D.C. is slowly starting to sift through the impact of Lambert’s rampage, one that prompted a massive police deployment, left behind six victims, displaced residents from the Metropole condominium on 15th Street NW, and raised uncomfortable questions about a man who was both an accomplished professional and deep into an emotionally fraught and expensive legal fight over mold and other issues in his seventh-floor penthouse.

The impact is especially deep for the victims and their friends and families. In one case, Minnesota mother Susan Hamerski, who was visiting D.C. for her daughter’s wedding, was shot in the face as she walked the newlywed’s dog, The Sun’s Martin Austermuhle reports.

For Jimmy’s circle of friends, the loss is painful. “He showed me life is fun, life is an adventure, take advantage of it, and if something makes you uncomfortable, try it once, and if it doesn’t work out, it doesn’t work out,” Daniel Prengel told The Sun’s Justice Covert and Nicole Belcastro about Stuart, a 46-year-old property manager at the building.

A new week is starting, but normalcy may still be tough to come by for many. The Washington Post reports that Metropole residents1 may remain displaced for the week to come, as repairs are done to address damage caused by water and police who had to search every unit during Thursday’s barricade. At the same time, people have been leaving notes of condolence and support outside the building and a neighboring bagel shop where some residents and gymgoers huddled during the shooting.

The Vida gym where the shooting started could reopen as soon as this weekend, its owners now say. But moving on won’t involve forgetting.

“Reading the notes of love and support from our neighbors brought me to tears,” wrote Vida founder David Von Storch. “D.C. isn’t just where politicians argue. It is our home. We work and live here. We share this loss and grieve together. Tomorrow we begin to pick up the pieces and the process of healing.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

East Potomac Park (3557x2371, AR: 1.50)
Swing and a miss: The East Potomac Golf Links remain open — for now. A federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from shuttering and redeveloping the course on Saturday, just a day before it was due to close.

In a daylong hearing Friday, administration officials argued that closing the course was necessary because of safety hazards caused by a deteriorating seawall, The Sun’s Derek Hawkins and Justice Covert report. The preservation groups suing them argued that reasoning was a flimsy cover for President Donald Trump’s plans to redesign the course and turn it into a championship-level golfing venue. The president posted on social media yesterday that his administration “will immediately appeal, on an expedited basis, this highly destructive and political decision of the judge.”

As the excitement of the midterm elections dies down, it’s time for the work to begin — and these politically minded Gen Z students are eager to organize. The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad profiles three young people from across the political spectrum who are pushing for change.

The National Guard wants to take a load off. It’s looking for D.C.-area cleaning companies who can provide daily wash-and-fold laundry service for military equipment, clothing, towels and bed linen at 13 hotels in which guard members are living during their deployment in D.C., The Sun’s Domonique King reports.






FROM VIRGINIA

Former Gov. Glenn Youngkin never finished enrolling Virginia in a new federal school voucher program. His successor, Gov. Abigail Spanberger, doesn’t believe the program will be beneficial for public school students and won’t finish the process this year, The Washington Post reports.





FROM MARYLAND

Lawmakers are concerned about how long it’s taking the state to investigate and clean up the more than 30,000 gallons of jet fuel that spilled from Joint Base Andrews into Piscataway Creek earlier this year, The Washington Post reports.





TRIVIA


Who is the only president to permanently settle in D.C. immediately after leaving office?

  1. Gerald Ford
  2. Theodore Roosevelt
  3. Woodrow Wilson
Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout out. The answer will be at the end of the newsletter tomorrow.





SPORTS

Audi Field crowd semifinal (4391x2927, AR: 1.50)
The Washington Spirit is headed to the NWSL final. Washington punched its ticket with a 2-1 win over the Utah Royals in Saturday’s semi, earning a chance to play for a league title on its home field next weekend. It will mark the franchise’s third straight championship match appearance, but The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri writes that this time feels different. Washington has breezed through its playoff run so far, giving players and fans hope that — after two straight championship defeats — the final outcome will be different, too.

Not long after the game ended, the grounds crew at Audi Field started clearing equipment (and fans) to make way for part two of the venue’s ambitious doubleheader: the Secretaries’ Cup. The Division III football rivalry, the source of a scheduling conflict that took days to sort, kicked off at 4:30. The Sun’s Emma Ruby and Emma Baccellieri report on the mixed emotions of the game.

On the other end of the soccer spectrum, D.C. United fired coach René Weiler over the weekend. Hired in July 2025, Weiler couldn’t change the fortunes of a floundering franchise that just completed its seventh consecutive losing season. Former Orlando City SC and FC Dallas coach Óscar Pareja has been hired as his replacement.

What’s wrong with the Wizards? Well, how much time do you have? Washington entered this season with a revamped roster and hopes to level up after years of futility. But, as The Sun’s Alex Schiffer reports, it’s been more of the same so far this season as the team’s new blend of young talent and veteran savvy has produced one of the league’s worst offenses and a mediocre defense.

What to Watch Today

NCAAM: Maryland vs. Alcorn State, 6 p.m. (BTN)NBA: Wizards vs. Grizzlies, 7 p.m. (Monumental)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Gaby Morera Di Núbila.

entries.title: Trump's Handpicked RNC Chair Is Under Scrutiny Over Hair and Makeup Services
entries.summary: Some Republican National Committee members want an audit of spending.
entries.content:
By Steve Peoples and Jill Colvin

NEW YORK — A nascent rebellion is underway against President Donald Trump's handpicked chairman at the Republican National Committee, and it’s already getting ugly.

Some members are calling for a forensic audit of spending decisions, including hair and makeup services for Trump and other officials, as well as the hiring of the daughter of Trump's former chief of staff. Feuding Republicans are leaking emails and opposition research on rival factions. The White House is threatening to cut off fundraising assistance if the rebels don’t fall in line.

The emerging fight, which will shape the 2028 presidential nominating contest, represents a rare challenge to Trump's dominance, even after the party's worst midterm performance in a generation. Despite the heavy losses, Republican leaders across Washington have shown little desire to move past Trump and have largely stood behind his most unpopular policies.

But inside the RNC, an organization of 168 members elected from every state who oversee the party’s national political operation, a small yet growing group is backing an attempt to depose Joe Gruters. Trump wants to keep him in charge.

The dissidents are rallying behind Kentucky’s KC Crosbie, the RNC's second-in-command, who launched her bid just two days after the Nov. 3 election in a letter that drew the fury of both the White House and Gruters' allies.

Crosbie remains a vocal Trump supporter who backs his “Make America Great Again” agenda, but her opponents view her gambit as a direct challenge to the president and his power.

“We have an obligation to serve the Republican Party the most effective way we can. And if all we do is say yes to what the White House wants, I’m not sure that’s doing what’s best for the Republican Party,” said RNC member Oscar Brock of Tennessee, who is supporting Crosbie’s candidacy. “Our job is to elect Republicans broadly, not to support one man all the time.”

He said that requires a change in leadership.

“There’s so much frustration that Chairman Gruters didn’t pull his weight in this election, that the RNC was far less effective than it should have been,” he said.

In her letter, Crosbie described the midterms as “a serious setback" and called for the RNC to provide “an honest account” of what went wrong.

“We should preserve what we built and be equally willing to confront where we fell short,” she wrote.

Crosbie declined to be interviewed. The leadership election will be held in January at the RNC’s winter meeting in Arizona.

Inside the Rebellion Against Gruters

It’s unclear how many RNC members will back Crosbie, although the number so far is believed to be small. Some would-be supporters privately acknowledge that they're worried about a backlash from the White House, especially with Stephen Miller taking over as Trump's new White House chief of staff. Others believe in the committee's tradition of having presidents pick their own party chiefs.

Gruters also has vocal backers.

Lauren LePage, an RNC member from Maine, praised the chairman's leadership and his efforts to help her father, Paul LePage, flip a congressional seat — a rare bright spot for Republicans this election cycle.

She described Gruters as “highly responsive” during the campaign and praised his “record-setting fundraising."

“From my perspective, as chairman, he did his job," she said, adding that Trump's endorsement is “something that the committee should take very seriously.”

Nevada Republican Party Chairman Michael McDonald called Crosbie a “dear friend," but said Trump is “the leader of our party” and “you always have to fall in line with the leader.”

“I don’t have a bad word to say about KC at all. It's just that the president wants to go with Joe Gruters," he said. “The president made his choice.”

The Republicans who have lined up behind Crosbie insist a leadership change is needed to send a clear message that the party will do things differently after losses even in conservative strongholds such as Texas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

Patti Lyman, an RNC member from Virginia, said it would be “catastrophic” and “insulting” to the party’s base “to keep the same leadership and pretend that we don’t need to do anything different, that we don’t need new players and a new plan.”

Lyman described Crosbie as “by far the best candidate currently running to lead the RNC forward to victory in 2028.”

Sue Cienki, an RNC committee member from Rhode Island, predicted that Crosbie would have the backing of at least two members from 10 states — for a total of 20 — at the committee's January meeting. That number is the minimum required for a successful nomination.

She insisted that she wouldn't be scared off by backlash from Trump or the White House, which has been actively lobbying RNC members.

“We should not be influenced by any one person or other. It’s our organization," Cienki said. “We have to hold an election, not a selection.”

Trump Is Furious With Crosbie

Trump and senior White House officials were livid about Crosbie’s Nov. 5 letter and the fact that they were given no heads-up.

During a White House meeting Nov. 6, Trump threatened to punish the RNC if members crossed him and said he would refuse to help the organization, including appearing at fundraisers or allowing his name and image to be used in mail and digital solicitations. That’s according to a senior White House official with direct knowledge of the meeting who was not authorized to publicly discuss the private gathering and spoke on condition of anonymity.

Such a threat would be catastrophic to the party because Trump remains its most effective money raiser.

An Axios story that first reported the threats was distributed via text message to all 168 RNC members.

The same senior White House official said staff convinced Trump that he should not go after Crosbie personally that day. Instead, he released a lengthy statement on his Truth Social social media platform hailing Gruters as a “MAGA Warrior” and giving him his “Complete and Total Endorsement.”

The leadership fight comes as Trump has shown no interest in relinquishing power

The Constitution bars Trump from seeking a third term, but he is expected to play a central role in picking the party's next presidential nominee. Trump's team contends that he remains the most popular Republican in the country, and House Republicans this week elected a slate of new leaders closely aligned with him.

The White House referred questions about the leadership fight to Trump’s Truth Social post.

The Party's Future Is at Stake

The RNC will oversee the party's presidential primary process, including setting the nominating calendar, the debate schedule, the national convention and the rules governing the selection of the White House candidate.

People close to Gruters, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations, said Crosbie’s campaign was “100% a challenge" to the president’s power and described the RNC as “the president’s political operation.”

Allies argued that a leadership change now would put the RNC at a severe disadvantage heading into the next presidential cycle because a new team would need time to get up to speed and they warned that friction between the president and the committee's leadership would curtail their ability to organize and raise money.

They also rejected Crosbie's call for a postelection review, which they said would do little more than rehash the past and put all their grievances on paper. Similar demands for a retrospective were a headache for Ken Martin, the embattled leader of the Democratic National Committee, after Trump won in 2024.

But they said Gruters has taken the criticism seriously and has been soliciting feedback to make adjustments heading into 2028.

Gruters spent much of this week holding private phone conversations with committee members. Those who participated in the calls said Gruters listened to their grievances but said little about what he would do differently.

Spending Faces Scrutiny

The opposition to Trump's choice to lead the RNC has little to do with Trump's leadership or policy decisions, according to nearly a half-dozen Crosbie supporters.

Instead, they focused on the RNC's spending decisions under Gruters. Republicans had a massive fundraising advantage and still lost the House and Senate.

“There’s clearly a groundswell of support for a forensic audit,” said Brock, the RNC member from Tennessee.

In a letter to RNC members sent Thursday night and obtained by The Associated Press, Gruters acknowledged concerns.

Gruters defended a $22,500 expenditure for hospitality space at the Presidents Cup, a golf event, saying it was offered to major donors and "resulted in $2.5 million in renewed contributions to the RNC.”

He also addressed concerns about “a brief contract” between the RNC and Caroline Wiles, a longtime Republican consultant who is the daughter of Susie Wiles, Trump's former chief of staff. Gruters said she was hired by his predecessor at the committee, Michael Whatley.

“While I have no reason to doubt Caroline Wiles’s value to the RNC or Chairman Whatley’s reasons for bringing her on, this was a brief six-month engagement that ended when I was elected Chairman,” he wrote.

Gruters also defended the RNC's decision to pay for “hair and make-up services” for senior White House officials, including Trump, Vice President JD Vance and former press secretary Karoline Leavitt.

“This was a request made of us so that the expense did not fall to taxpayers,” Gruters wrote. He said the beneficiaries “generously gave so much of their limited time and energies to help the RNC this cycle” and “did not ask for much of us in return, so we felt this was a request we could accommodate.”

Gruters promised to provide members “honest and direct answers to concerns raised” as conversations continue.

“I pledge to listen and learn from you about what happened in the field,” he wrote, “so together we can move forward stronger than ever.”

entries.title: House Democrats Are Prepping Their AI Bills — Without Republicans
entries.summary: The regulatory proposals go further than Republicans and the AI industry have been wanting to go in previous negotiations.
entries.content:
House Democrats, preparing to take back control of Congress, are planning to push artificial intelligence regulation further than their Republican counterparts — and the AI industry — have been willing to go.

Rep. Lori Trahan (D-Massachusetts) is reworking the FRONTIER Act to make clear that state regulations could go further than federal standards, according to Trahan’s spokesperson, Francis Grubar.

Trahan originally negotiated the bill with Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-California) to set safety rules for companies building the most powerful AI models. But that bipartisan bill served as a ceiling on regulation and barred states from adopting or enforcing new requirements on AI developers in three areas tied to catastrophic risk: disclosing how they manage those risks, submitting to outside audits and reporting safety incidents to the government.

Trahan has worked on the rewrite alone so far, Grubar said, “to reflect additional feedback on areas where it could be strengthened.” Her office is expected to reveal the changes in the coming week, with incident reporting and audits on recursive self-improvement being a focus.

The lawmaker hasn't taken the revised effort to Obernolte yet. Obernolte's office did not respond to a request for comment.

Trahan’s forthcoming changes to the FRONTIER Act show the extent to which Democrats feel they have a mandate from voters to address the rise of AI and data centers. It also sets up a fight over bipartisan tech regulation in the next Congress, where Democrats have a sizable majority in the House but still must compromise with Republicans in the Senate.

At the center of the debate is preemption, when federal law overrides state law, which has been the primary fight over AI regulation so far. The White House and congressional Republicans spent the past year pushing to block state AI laws. President Donald Trump’s December 2025 executive order created a Justice Department task force to challenge state AI laws and threatened to withhold broadband funding from states with "onerous" laws.

Offering any kind of federal standard for AI regulation, like the FRONTIER Act, was already a concession for Republicans.

"Preemption with a federal replacement was not a discussion the Republican Party was having in the last year," Adam Conner, the vice president of technology policy at the Center for American Progress, told The Washington Sun. "It was preempt without any sort of replacement, and that was, I think, a no-go for most people."

But Democrats appear ready to push regulation further.

It’s not just Trahan that wants Congress to establish a regulatory floor. Rep. Ted Lieu (D-California), who co-chairs House Democrats' AI commission and is writing his own bill, said he is also going in that direction.

"My staff and I have been working with stakeholders on a strong AI testing, auditing and disclosure bill that has preemption as a floor, not a ceiling," Lieu wrote in a social media post.

AI policy in the House would likely end up before Rep. Frank Pallone (D-New Jersey), who’s currently the top Democrat on the Energy and Commerce Committee. Pallone has backed a national moratorium on data centers.

If implemented, such laws would allow for AI regulations in California, which took effect in this past January, and in New York and Illinois, which would take effect Jan. 1, 2027, to move forward.

The politics have shifted since the FRONTIER Act was first written. In NBC News exit polling, 56% of voters said that AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress.

“Those are crazy numbers for technology. We’ve never been on the map with voters,” said

Chris MacKenzie of Americans for Responsible Innovation, an AI safety group.

MacKenzie said states have been the fastest to respond as AI changes month to month. Capping them now would be “fundamentally short-sighted,” he told The Sun.

The new majority wouldn’t need Republican leaders to bring AI bills to the floor. But Senate Democrats would be short of the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster, and any bill still faces a possible veto from Trump.

Preemption is only one piece of a crowded AI agenda for this incoming Congress. Democrats are also facing fights over data centers’ power costs, AI chip exports, children’s online safety and AI’s effect on jobs.

“I think the biggest challenge is not necessarily about the House Democrats themselves, but that AI is such a general-purpose technology that’s going to touch all sorts of things,” Conner said.

Safety and consumer groups are also lobbying over who gets the gavels. More than 50 of them asked Democratic leaders to weigh members' positions on AI when assigning committee chairs.

MacKenzie expects more than one bill: “I would actually expect to see a few different competing proposals.”
